analysis.one_liner: Makes truck drivers eligible for overtime pay after a full workweek.
analysis.headline: The bill to extend overtime pay to truck drivers was introduced by a Republican with Democratic support, but has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee without a hearing or vote since its referral in March 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike a decades-old carve-out in the Fair Labor Standards Act that exempts most truck drivers from federal overtime rules. Under current law, employees of regulated motor carriers get no time-and-a-half pay no matter how long their week runs, even though many routinely work 60 to 70 hours. Deleting that exemption would make those drivers eligible for overtime like most other American workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers employed by regulated motor carriers, a workforce of millions that is among the most likely to work very long weeks for modest pay. They would gain a legal right to time-and-a-half pay for every hour past 40 in a week, something they are currently denied by the exemption this bill removes [S2]. The bill was introduced by Rep. Jefferson Van Drew (R-NJ) with Rep. Mark Takano (D-CA) and drew cosponsors from both parties [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Deletes paragraph (1) of Section 13(b) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that exempts motor carrier employees from overtime pay requirements, making those truckers eligible for time-and-a-half after 40 hours in a week.
Targets the exemption that leaves truck drivers — a workforce that commonly works 60-plus-hour weeks — without any overtime premium, unlike most other hourly workers covered by federal wage law.
Attracted bipartisan sponsorship: a Republican introduced it with a Democratic original cosponsor, and the 3 cosponsors include 2 Democrats and 1 Republican.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and motor carriers, whose payroll costs would rise wherever drivers now work more than 40 hours a week. Some of that cost would likely be passed on to the businesses that ship freight and, ultimately, to consumer prices. Carriers might also respond by restructuring pay or capping hours rather than paying overtime, which could blunt gains for some drivers.

drawbacks.text: Operating costs for motor carriers would rise, and some of that would likely be passed through as higher freight rates to shippers, small businesses, and consumers.

Because federal safety rules already cap how many hours a driver can be on the road, carriers might respond to an overtime mandate by cutting hours instead of paying time-and-a-half — and since many drivers are paid by the mile rather than by the hour, a shorter week could actually reduce take-home pay for drivers who today earn more by running long weeks.
Small and marginal carriers with thin margins would face the same payroll increase as large fleets, and some could exit the market, concentrating the industry further.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: a right to overtime for a big, long-hours, modestly paid workforce that has been excluded from it since the exemption was written into the 1938 law. The costs — higher freight operating expenses and possible price pass-through — are genuine but spread across the economy. The bigger design question is whether truckers' per-mile pay structure plus federal hours caps would let carriers blunt the benefit by shortening weeks, which is a fair objection an honest supporter should acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it stalled but technically alive until this Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew (R-NJ) introduced the Guaranteeing Overtime for Truckers Act on March 6, 2025, joined by Rep. Mark Takano (D-CA) as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which holds jurisdiction over federal wage law.
The bill picked up 3 cosponsors — 2 Democrats and 1 Republican — and has had no further action since referral; it has never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, motor carriers are ahead: the overtime exemption stays in place and truck drivers' pay rules are unchanged. Truck drivers have gained nothing yet, and the bipartisan sponsorship has produced no legislative movement.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with a Democratic original cosponsor and a 2-to-1 Democratic-to-Republican cosponsor split — but with only 4 total members and no votes on record, the partisan shape of broader support is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would end the overtime exemption these employers currently rely on, raising payroll costs for drivers who work past 40 hours. Because many drivers routinely run 60- to 70-hour weeks at straight time, this is a direct transfer from carrier margins to driver paychecks — which is why carriers' interest in the bill runs against their own employees' pay.

Businesses that move goods by truck would likely face higher freight rates if carriers pass through overtime costs. The effect on their customers is a modest price increase spread across the economy, not a concentrated loss.

analysis.trajectory: Bills to repeal the motor carrier overtime exemption have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses and none has reached a floor vote. With only 3 cosponsors, no committee action more than a year after referral, and referral to a committee controlled by the opposing agenda, the most likely path is that this bill dies quietly in committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
